```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4, dpi = 72)
library(rmoriebricklayer)
```

A reform reaches some places before others: a new criminal procedure rolled out district by
district, a policing program adopted city by city, a ward boundary redrawn. Agencies publish the
outcomes as counts or rates by place and period. This vignette covers the designs that turn such a
table into an estimate of the reform's effect, with honest uncertainty. Each estimator gives the
same answer as the reference implementation (`fixest`, `did`, `bacondecomp`) to rounding error,
and none of them needs a package outside base R.

The examples use `polex()`: twenty districts in four regions over 36 months, with a
reform that reaches the regions in three stages (months 13, 19 and 25) and never reaches the
fourth. The numbers are made up, with a known effect: the reform lowers the crime rate by 3.

```{r data}
p <- polex()
head(p)
```

## Difference in differences

`plndid()` fits the two-way fixed-effects regression, with standard errors clustered by unit
(or any coarser grouping), and reports the effect relative to the comparison units' mean before
the reform:

```{r did}
plndid(p, "district", "month", "crmrate", "reformed")
```

## Before any model

`cohtrnd()` shows each adoption cohort's outcome around its adoption, scaled to 1 just
before it:

```{r trends, fig.height = 3.5}
plot(cohtrnd(p, "district", "month", "crmrate", "refmonth", win = c(-10, 10)))
```

## Leads and lags

`evstudy()` estimates the effect period by period around adoption. The leads (periods before
adoption) should be near zero; the joint test of that is printed below the table:

```{r event, fig.height = 3.5}
es <- evstudy(p, "district", "month", "crmrate", "refmonth", leads = 4, lags = 6)
es
plot(es)
```

## Staggered adoption

When districts adopt at different times, the two-way estimate uses districts already treated as
controls for later ones. `bacondcmp()` shows how much weight those comparisons get:

```{r bacon, fig.height = 3.5}
b <- bacondcmp(p, "district", "month", "crmrate", "reformed")
tapply(b$weight, b$type, sum)
plot(b)
```

`stgatt()` avoids them: each cohort is compared only with districts not yet treated
(Callaway and Sant'Anna), or the regression has a coefficient for every cohort and period
(Wooldridge). The bootstrap resamples whole districts:

```{r cs, fig.height = 3.5}
s <- stgatt(p, "district", "month", "crmrate", "refmonth", reps = 99, seed = 1)
s$overall
plot(s)
```

For a treatment that can switch off as well as on, `swtdid()` compares the units that
switch with those that do not, in the period they switch, with a placebo one period earlier:

```{r switching}
swtdid(p, "district", "month", "crmrate", "reformed", reps = 99, seed = 1)
```

## Inference from the assignment

With four regions there are only 24 ways to assign the three stages and the never-treated region.
`perminf()` tries every one, and gives the share at least as extreme as the real
assignment. With two outcomes it also gives Westfall and Young's stepdown p-values, which hold the
chance of any false positive at the nominal level:

```{r perm, fig.height = 3}
r <- perminf(p, "district", "month", c("crmrate", "arrrate"), "refmonth",
                           cl = "region")
r
plot(r, type = "histogram")
```

`loounit()` checks that no single district drives the estimate:

```{r loo, fig.height = 3.5}
plot(loounit(p, "district", "month", "crmrate", "reformed"))
```

Several outcomes at once, in the style of a Stata event-study figure:

```{r grid, fig.height = 3.5}
plotevgrid(list(
  "Crime rate" = es,
  "Arrest rate" = evstudy(p, "district", "month", "arrrate", "refmonth", leads = 4,
                              lags = 6)), style = "stata")
```

## Counts

For counts, `plnpois()` gives the effect as a rate ratio, with the population as exposure:

```{r pois}
plnpois(p, "district", "month", "crimes", "reformed", offset = "logpop")
```

## One treated place

`synctl()` builds a weighted average of untreated places that tracks the treated one
before the reform, and runs the same method on each untreated place as a placebo:

```{r synth, fig.height = 3.5}
p13 <- p[is.na(p$refmonth) | p$district == "D13", ]
sc <- synctl(p13, "district", "month", "crmrate", "D13", adopt = 13)
sc
plot(sc)
```

## Measures for justice data

Three measures prepare the outcomes these designs take:

- `sevidx()` combines offence rates, weighted by each offence's severity (for example its
  mean statutory sentence);
- `piperate()` gives the rate at which one stage of the justice process follows another,
  with the input's window set before the outcome's, because cases take time;
- `cmlrisk()` gives the chance of a first arrest (or conviction, or placement) by each
  age, from first events and the population.

For place-based designs, `bufasgn()` marks places near a site as treated, places near a
comparison point and far from every site as the comparison, and excludes the rest.

```{r measures}
d <- data.frame(city = rep(c("A", "B"), each = 3), year = 2024,
                offence = rep(c("homicide", "robbery", "burglary"), 2),
                n = c(5, 120, 300, 2, 90, 410), pop = rep(c(250000, 180000), each = 3))
sevidx(d, "city", "year", "offence", "n",
               w = c(homicide = 25, robbery = 8, burglary = 4), pop = "pop")
cmlrisk(16:20, c(900, 1400, 1700, 1600, 1400), rep(1e5, 5))
```

## Doing better than the original designs

Published applications of these designs often share a few weaknesses, and each has a remedy here.

**Few clusters.** A reform assigned to a handful of districts gives cluster-robust tests that
reject too often. `wcb()` gives an honest p-value and interval; with four
clusters it says plainly that nothing can be rejected at 5%:

```{r wild}
wcb(p, "district", "month", "crmrate", "reformed", cl = "region")
```

**Doubts about parallel trends.** `tse()` asks how large a departure from
parallel trends, relative to the largest seen before adoption, would make the effect vanish:

```{r sens}
tse(es, seed = 1)
```

**Covariates that differ between groups.** `stgatt()` with `covariates` is doubly robust
(use covariates fixed before treatment: one the reform moves, such as arrests, is a bad
control). `plndml()` lets a machine learner fit the confounding with fixed effects, and
`mtchdid()` matches units on their pre-reform paths before differencing:

```{r covs}
set.seed(4)
p$x1 <- rnorm(20)[match(p$district, unique(p$district))]
stgatt(p, "district", "month", "crmrate", "refmonth", covs = "x1", reps = 49,
              seed = 1)$overall
m <- mtchdid(p, "district", "month", "crmrate", "refmonth", ratio = 2)
m$estimate
```

**A single treated place, or a few.** `syndid()` weights both comparison units and
pre-periods:

```{r sdid}
syndid(p13, "district", "month", "crmrate", "refmonth", reps = 50, seed = 1)
```

**Null results without a measure of power.** `plnpwr()` simulates the design on the
untreated data and gives the minimum detectable effect:

```{r power, fig.height = 3.5}
pw <- plnpwr(p[p$month <= 12, ], "district", "month", "crmrate", ntrt = 10,
                  adopt = 7:10, eff = c(0, 0.5, 1, 1.5), reps = 40, seed = 1)
pw
plot(pw)
```

## Indigenous examples

The methods here need a panel: units observed over time, some treated at a known date.
The bundled Indigenous tables are repeated cross-sections of published estimates, so the
before-and-after comparison they support is the change in a gap, with its interval:

```{r indigenous-policy}
hi <- indiex("health")
x <- hi[hi$age == "Total, 18 years and over" &
          hi$indicator == "Perceived mental health, very good or excellent", ]
gaps <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(x, x$period), function(p) {
  cbind(period = p$period[1],
        indgap(p, "group", "estimate", "lower", "upper")[
          , c("group", "difference", "diflo", "difup")])
}))
rownames(gaps) <- NULL
gaps
```

Perceived mental health fell for every group between the two cycles; whether the gaps
moved is read from the intervals, not the point estimates.

## Acknowledgements

These designs are those of the empirical work of Professor Angela Zorro Medina (University of
Toronto) on criminal-procedure reform, political dynasties, police stops and the cumulative risk of
criminal justice outcomes. The estimators themselves are the standard ones of the literature cited
on each help page.
